Baby & Child

ADHD assessment and treatment: when to seek help

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

There is no single best birthday for starting ADHD care, and no deadline after which help stops working. The useful question is whether a child's difficulties are persistent and affecting daily life. Assessment can clarify what is happening; support can then be matched to their development and needs. If concerns arise later in childhood, adolescence or adulthood, they still deserve attention.

Look for a pattern, not one restless afternoon

ADHD can involve difficulty sustaining attention, managing impulses or regulating activity. A child may repeatedly lose belongings, miss details, struggle to finish tasks, interrupt or find waiting unusually difficult. Some children are mainly inattentive and may appear quiet or dreamy. Being able to concentrate on a favourite activity does not settle the question either way.

These behaviours also occur in children without ADHD, especially when they are young, tired or under stress. Clinicians consider what is expected for the child's developmental stage, how often difficulties occur and whether they interfere with learning, relationships or everyday tasks. A symptom checklist is a starting point for discussion, not a diagnosis or a measure of how hard a child is trying.

Seek advice when difficulties interfere with everyday life

Contact your child's usual healthcare professional when concerns persist or cause meaningful problems at home, in childcare or at school. You do not need to wait for repeated school failure. Very active behaviour before age five can be part of ordinary development, but substantial difficulties still deserve assessment and support. Ask which professional or service evaluates children of this age locally.

Bring examples rather than a label: what happened, where, how often and what made the situation easier or harder. Include the child's strengths and perspective. Information from teachers or other caregivers can be useful, including when their observations differ from yours. While waiting for assessment, ask what practical support is available; a diagnosis need not be the first conversation about a child's needs.

An assessment brings together several kinds of information

There is no single blood test, scan or questionnaire that establishes ADHD. A suitably trained clinician reviews development, health, behaviour and functioning, usually using information from the family and another setting. Depending on local services and expertise, assessment may involve a paediatrician, primary-care professional, psychologist or psychiatrist. A computer-based attention task, where used, does not replace the wider clinical assessment.

Diagnostic criteria require a persistent pattern, including symptoms for at least six months, several symptoms before age twelve, and difficulties across at least two settings. The clinician also assesses impairment and whether another explanation fits better. These criteria are not instructions to delay seeking help for six months. An older child's assessment can draw on earlier reports and history rather than assuming that later recognition means the symptoms are new.

Check for other needs and avoid blaming the family

Sleep problems, anxiety, depression, learning difficulties and hearing or vision problems can affect attention or behaviour. Some can resemble ADHD; others can occur alongside it. Tell the clinician about sleep, school progress, recent changes and existing health conditions. Finding another difficulty does not automatically rule ADHD in or out, and treating only one problem may leave important needs unmet.

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with a strong genetic contribution and multiple influences. Its cause cannot usually be reduced to one event or parenting decision. Families do not need to prove that they have been perfect parents before requesting help. Parent training is recommended because adults can help a child practise useful skills and shape supportive routines, not because the diagnosis establishes parental fault.

For younger children, start with coached parent support

For children younger than six, US guidance recommends parent training in behaviour management before medication. A trained therapist teaches caregivers practical strategies and reviews how these work between sessions. This is more than telling a family to be stricter. It can involve clear instructions, consistent responses and positive reinforcement, adapted to the child's abilities and the family's circumstances.

Ask whether the programme includes practice, feedback and help adjusting an approach that is not working. Other caregivers can learn the same methods. Play therapy or talking with the child alone is not an established substitute for this treatment of core ADHD symptoms in young children, although therapy may address other emotional needs. If appropriate training is unavailable, tell the clinician so that access problems are included in care planning.

School-age children and teenagers may need combined care

For children aged six and older, recommended care commonly combines medication with behavioural support and help at school. The balance depends on the child's difficulties, preferences and response. Agree on a few meaningful goals, such as completing a morning routine or participating more comfortably in lessons. Treatment should help functioning and wellbeing, rather than simply making a child quieter.

School support remains relevant even when medication helps. Keep communication between the family, clinician and school focused on the agreed needs and progress. As children become teenagers, include them directly in decisions and discuss concerns about treatment, independence and privacy. A plan that suited an earlier school year may need changing as demands increase; continued difficulties are a reason to review care, not to assign blame.

Medicine decisions depend on the child and the formulation

Stimulant and non-stimulant medicines can reduce ADHD symptoms, but benefits and unwanted effects differ between individuals. Medication does not replace every skill, relationship or educational support a child needs. Ask what improvement to look for, which adverse effects to report and when the prescription will be reviewed. Do not use another person's medicine or change the prescribed dose yourself.

Preschool prescribing requires particular care. In selected younger children with serious continuing impairment despite behavioural treatment, a clinician may consider medication; rules and specialist requirements differ between countries. The FDA warned in 2025 about greater weight-loss risk with extended-release amphetamine and methylphenidate products in children under six, for whom those products are not approved. This is not a statement that every ADHD medicine or formulation has the same age approval.

Build review and safe medicine handling into the plan

Follow-up should compare benefits with problems such as reduced appetite, disturbed sleep or mood changes. The clinician may monitor growth, weight, pulse and blood pressure, with the schedule tailored to treatment and guidance. Report changes rather than quietly abandoning care or accepting troublesome effects as unavoidable. Ask how to contact the prescriber between appointments and when the overall treatment plan will be reconsidered.

Prescription stimulants also carry risks of misuse, addiction and overdose. Keep them securely stored, never share them and use them only as prescribed. Discuss safe disposal of unused medicine and any concern about someone taking or requesting it. If an overdose or accidental ingestion is suspected, seek urgent poison-service or emergency medical advice. Do not wait for a routine ADHD appointment.

Everyday support helps; a special diet is not a substitute

Predictable routines, short instructions and manageable steps can make daily tasks easier. Notice progress and praise specific efforts, with goals the child can realistically reach. Regular sleep, enjoyable physical activity and nutritious meals support general health. These are parts of a supportive environment, not proof that a family can cure ADHD by perfecting a schedule or choosing a particular sport.

Do not assume that iron, omega-3 supplements or removing sugar and additives will treat ADHD. NICE does not recommend routine fatty-acid supplements or general additive-elimination diets for this purpose. If a particular food seems linked to symptoms, discuss a record of the pattern with a clinician and, when appropriate, a dietitian. A confirmed nutritional problem needs its own assessment; restrictive diets should not replace established care.

There is no golden-age deadline for getting help

Early recognition can make support available sooner, but it does not establish a universal treatment window before age five or six. Nor should families assume that every child will simply grow out of ADHD. Symptoms and their impact can change over time, and difficulties may continue into adulthood. The appropriate response is ongoing assessment of needs, with care adjusted as circumstances change.

At the next appointment, ask what supports the diagnosis, what alternatives were considered and which first steps fit your child. Agree on who will coordinate care and how progress will be judged. If a plan is not helping, bring concrete examples to the review. Seeking another assessment later is still worthwhile; the child's present needs matter more than whether an earlier opportunity was missed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Assess persistent impairment across settings and consider alternative or coexisting conditions.

Match treatment to developmental age, individual needs and local prescribing guidance.

Review functioning, benefits and adverse effects over time; avoid fixed treatment deadlines and unsupported dietary promises.

How BeMama can help

Use this guide to prepare for an assessment or treatment review. BeMama cannot diagnose ADHD, select a medicine or determine a dose for your child.

When to seek help

Discuss troublesome symptoms or medicine effects with your child's clinician. Do not share prescriptions or change treatment yourself. Suspected overdose or accidental ingestion needs urgent poison-service or emergency medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Persistent difficulties and their impact matter more than a single symptom or birthday.
  • Assessment uses developmental history, information across settings and consideration of other conditions.
  • Parent behaviour training is the usual first treatment for younger children.
  • Medicines require individual selection, follow-up and safe storage; do not share or adjust them yourself.
  • Support remains worthwhile in later childhood, adolescence and adulthood.

Frequently asked questions

Which signs might suggest ADHD?

Persistent inattention, losing things, difficulty completing tasks, impulsive interruptions or unusually high activity may raise concern when they interfere with daily life. Some children mainly struggle with attention. Similar behaviours have other explanations, so a checklist or isolated incident cannot diagnose ADHD.

Can ADHD affect adult life?

Yes. Difficulties may continue and affect organisation, work, relationships or wellbeing, although the pattern varies. These outcomes are not inevitable, and support is available in adulthood. A child's diagnosis does not predict a fixed future.

What causes ADHD?

Genetics plays an important role, alongside other influences on development. There is no single cause that explains every person, and assessment is not a search for a parenting mistake. Family support is useful regardless of whether relatives have a diagnosis.

What is the best age to start treatment?

There is no universal golden age or deadline. Seek advice when persistent difficulties affect daily life. Treatment should fit developmental age and need: younger children usually start with parent behaviour training, while older children may benefit from combined approaches.

Must a young child take medicine?

No. Parent training is usually the first approach. A clinician may consider medication for selected children with substantial continuing impairment, following local guidance and age-specific prescribing requirements. Do not assume that all products have the same approval or risk profile.

Can a diet or supplement replace ADHD treatment?

No special diet or supplement should be assumed to replace established care. Discuss suspected food-related patterns or nutritional problems with a qualified professional rather than starting a restrictive diet or routine supplementation yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
